extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
extraction.publisher: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
extraction.citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A total of 200 participants contributed to the dataset, with 188 retained after post-processing. Participants were equipped with six audio sensors simultaneously and recorded in a controlled environment. The recording process consisted of four steps performed consecutively for each participant: (1) speech-clean: participant reads sentences from French Wikipedia for 15 minutes; (2) speechless-noisy: participant remains silent for 2 minutes and 24 seconds in a noisy environment; (3) speechless-clean: participant remains silent for 54 seconds in complete silence; (4) speech-noisy: final phase of 54 seconds with noise from in-house ambisonic recordings. All six sensor signals were recorded simultaneously using a Zoom F8n field recorder at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution. A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with a total of 28,471 sentences. The post-processing filtering excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences. Issues included mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, filters were not triggered.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Text for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set, with a focus on noise classes relevant to BCM applications such as battlefield and industrial environments. In-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics were also used. Audio was recorded using six sensors simultaneously: a headset microphone (Shure WH20XLR), forehead accelerometer (Knowles BU23173-000), in-ear soft foam microphone (Knowles FG-23329-P07), in-ear rigid earpiece microphone (Knowles SPH1642HT5H), throat microphone (iXradio XVTM822D-D35), and temple vibration pickup (AKG C411), all recorded via a Zoom F8n field recorder.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Noise spatialization was carried out using the ambitools library and rendered by a spherical array with a radius of 1.07 meters made up of 56 loudspeakers. Audio Set noise samples were spatialized using a plane wave model from random fixed positions uniformly distributed on the sphere. Voice Activity Detection (VAD) timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% in training, 10% in development/validation, and 10% in test set, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A series of three automatic filters were applied to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies: (1) PER filter: discards audio samples where Phoneme Error Rate > 10%, computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; (2) SNR filter: verifies sensor functioning by checking that SNR[i,j] = Lspeech_50[i,j] - Lsilence_50[i,j] > 1.5 dB; (3) Sensitivity drift filter: checks that Lspeech_50[i,j] > Lsilence_50[i] to detect sensitivity drift. Only speech-clean samples passing all three filters were added to the dataset. All other subsets were included if the corresponding participant's speech-clean subset was not empty. Text was normalized by lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the IPA phonemizer from the CoML lab, with manual transcription for unrecognized words.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Textual transcriptions were sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice and filtered to exclude proper names (except common first names, French town/region names, and country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. Manual phonetic transcription was performed for words unrecognized by the phonemizer (e.g., 'algorithme'). Recording condition annotations were also included.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Text phonemizer of the CoML lab (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.03958); whisper-timestamped model for voice activity detection and word timestamp alignment
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The whisper-timestamped model was used to derive phonetic transcriptions from Whisper's output, which were compared to labeled phonetic transcriptions using Levenshtein distance to compute Phoneme Error Rate (PER). Samples with PER > 10% were discarded to ensure high-quality labels. Top phonetic confusions were analyzed per sensor to understand acoustic properties.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available on HuggingFace under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The dataset is versioned (revision 071945b referenced in citation). The GitHub repository https://github.com/jhauret/vibravox contains associated code.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are collected. Age statistics show female participants with mean age 25.9 years (range 19-59) and male participants with mean age 31.4 years (range 18-82). The dataset contains voice recordings which are biometric data. All necessary measures were taken to protect privacy including informed consent, anonymization, and encryption of data during storage and analysis.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with applications in military operations, industrial settings, voice commands, and vital sign monitoring. Speaker verification capabilities could be used for access control and intelligence gathering in military contexts. The dataset could enable development of voice command systems for heavy machinery operation, ensuring safety protocols. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants to increase representativeness and inclusivity.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is in French only, restricting applicability to French language research. The participant pool consists of 97 female and 91 male speakers aged 18-82, with a deliberate effort for gender balance. The Lombard effect (speakers increasing vocal effort in noisy conditions) means reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on actual values. Some participants had ear canals too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, which could affect results for those sensors.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is exclusively in French. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes as it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. The temple vibration pickup has a very small bandwidth (barely recording speech above 1500 Hz). Some in-ear microphone recordings may be affected by inadequate acoustic sealing for certain ear canal anatomies. The assumption that speakers produce speech at the same loudness in both quiet and noisy environments (used for SNR calculations) is violated by the Lombard effect. The dataset, while large, may not comprehensively cover all real-world acoustic scenarios.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation for speech enhancement (bandwidth extension), automatic speech recognition (speech-to-phonemes), and speaker verification tasks. The speech-clean subset is the primary training resource. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes. The speechless-clean subset can be used for heart rate tracking or analyzing noise properties of sensors. The speechless-noisy subset can be used for data augmentation by mixing with speech-clean recordings to simulate noisy conditions while retaining a clean reference.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male); female mean age 25.9 years (range 19-59), male mean age 31.4 years (range 18-82); all participants are French speakers; a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model (based on Whisper with dynamic time warping applied to cross-attention weights) for voice activity detection and word timestamp alignment; text phonemizer of the CoML lab for IPA phonetic transcription generation
